title: The Schedule Explosion
primary_metric: total idle GPU-minutes wasted by each scheduling strategy when sequencing Vantage Compute's six-job pilot batch through its shared model-loading pipeline -- the largest batch size at which The Full Sweep (Option A, exhaustive search over every possible job ordering) is still computationally checkable at all -- compared against The Greedy Queue (Option B, the nearest-neighbor heuristic rule already in production); extended in Challenge 3 to realistic 12-to-20-job nightly batches where The Full Sweep's own search time explodes past Vantage's eight-hour nightly batch window entirely

options.A: The Full Sweep -- commit to always finding the true, provably optimal job ordering by exhaustively checking every possible ordering of that night's batch
options.B: The Greedy Queue -- keep the fast nearest-neighbor rule already in production, accepting a calculable, bounded amount of extra idle time in exchange for a schedule that finishes instantly at any job count

sources.claim: The number of feasible orderings/solutions for a job-scheduling problem of n jobs is n!, and job-scheduling problems built on this fact are formally classified as computationally hard (NP-hard)
sources.title: Computational Optimization Open Textbook -- "Job shop scheduling"
sources.note: Primary academic source (a Cornell engineering-course-hosted optimization reference). States directly: 'There are n! feasible solutions for a job shop scheduling problem, therefore there are 4! = 24 feasible solutions for this example.' This is the pure-math fact the entire case is built on -- no proprietary or company-specific data needed.

deliverables.text: A factorial table: for each job count n listed in Appendix B (4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 18, and 20), evaluate n! -- the number of possible orderings of a batch of that size -- showing your method in full for at least three of the values.

Using Appendix C's assumed schedule-search speed, convert each of the D1 values into the total time a complete Full-Sweep search of that job count's orderings would take, and compare each one to Vantage's fixed eight-hour nightly batch window (Appendix B). State, with arithmetic shown, the largest job count at which The Full Sweep still finishes inside that window, and the smallest job count at which it does not.

For Appendix A's six-job pilot batch: restate the D1 value for 6! and confirm it is small enough for a real exhaustive search to actually examine every ordering, then carry out that exhaustive search to find The Full Sweep's true-optimal total idle time. Separately, apply The Greedy Queue's nearest-neighbor rule (Appendix D) to the same six jobs to find its total idle time. Report both totals and the percent margin between them, with arithmetic shown.

A written explanation, referencing at least two specific job-count/search-time pairs from the D2 table, of why Vantage's team cannot simply "wait for faster computers" to make The Full Sweep work at realistic nightly job counts. The explanation must state, in the student's own words, what a factorial is and why it grows the way it does.

An original visual display (a bar or line chart, using a logarithmic vertical scale) plotting job count against either n! or total Full-Sweep search time, across all of the D1/D2 job counts, showing the shape of the explosion.

appendices.title: Vantage's Six-Job Pilot Batch: Switchover-Cost Matrix
Vantage's Batch Sizes, Today and As The Fleet Grows

balance.argument_a: On the one batch size small enough to actually check exhaustively -- Vantage's real six-job pilot batch -- The Full Sweep is provably, calculably better: it finds the true-optimal ordering, and that ordering wastes real, measurably less idle time than The Greedy Queue's heuristic ordering on the exact same six jobs. This is not a guess or an approximation; it is the mathematically best possible answer for that batch, verified by checking every single one of the 6! = 720 possible orderings. If Vantage only ever ran six-job batches, there would be no real argument for anything else.
balance.argument_b: The whole point of a nightly scheduler is that it has to produce a schedule every single night, at whatever job count that night's batch actually has -- and Appendix B's own numbers show that Vantage's typical batch is already 12 jobs, twice the pilot batch's 6, heading toward 18-20 within the year as the fleet grows (grounded in real, publicly announced GPU-fleet growth, SEE APPENDIX E). At 12 jobs, an exhaustive Full-Sweep search still finishes in about 48 seconds -- but at 15 jobs it takes about 36.3 hours, more than 4 times Vantage's own 8-hour nightly window, and at 18-20 jobs it takes 20 to 7,709 years. A strategy that cannot even finish computing an answer some nights is not a real strategy for those nights, no matter how good its answer is on the 1 night out of many small enough for it to finish.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |idle_time(Greedy Queue) - idle_time(Full Sweep)| / idle_time(Greedy Queue), computed on Appendix A's six-job pilot batch (the only batch size in this case where a true exhaustive search over all 6! = 720 orderings is actually carried out). Full Sweep's true-optimal total idle time = 62 minutes (verified by sensitivity_model.py's exhaustive search over all 720 orderings of Appendix A's switchover-cost matrix). Greedy Queue's nearest-neighbor total idle time = 72 minutes (verified by sensitivity_model.py's nearest-neighbor simulation on the same matrix, starting from the LLM Fine-Tune job). margin = |72 - 62| / 72 = 10 / 72 = 13.9%. This is within the SPEC SS2 target 8-15% band and well inside the 20% hard cap. This margin describes only the six-job pilot batch -- it is not, and is not claimed to be, the margin at realistic nightly job counts (12-20 jobs), where The Full Sweep cannot be run to completion at all inside the eight-hour batch window (see case.json.derived and FACILITATOR.md for the full D2 feasibility-crossing arithmetic).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Appendix A's switchover-cost matrix (idle minutes per job-to-job transition)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Grounded in the real, benchmarked AWS range for AI model-loading time on a GPU node (roughly 1 to 8 minutes, S3), extended somewhat higher on some pairs to represent a full training-job environment switch (new container image + new dataset mount + new checkpoint), a larger operation than loading one inference model.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The margin between the two strategies on the six-job pilot batch is sensitive to the relative differences within this matrix, though not to its overall scale.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Appendix C's assumed schedule-search evaluation rate
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public benchmark exists for Vantage's own not-yet-built exhaustive schedule-search code. A conservative rate for a simple compiled loop summing lookup-table values per ordering, well within general modern hardware throughput.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Changing this value shifts exactly which job count crosses from feasible to infeasible inside the eight-hour window, but a factorial's growth guarantees some crossing point exists regardless of the exact rate chosen.

modeling_assumptions.basis: A round, representative overnight batch window, common in batch-computing operations generally, not tied to any named real provider's published schedule.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: A shorter or longer window changes exactly which job count first exceeds it, but not the underlying factorial growth rate.

derived.notes: Figures computed by sensitivity_model.py (exhaustive search + nearest-neighbor simulation over Appendix A's matrix, and the factorial/time table over Appendix B's job counts), kept here so FACILITATOR.md's Guide Notes stay checkable against a value of record.
derived.feasibility_crossing: Largest job count still inside the 8-hour (28,800-second) window: n=12 (~48 seconds). Smallest job count that exceeds it: n=15 (~130,767 seconds, ~36.3 hours).
